storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — high pressure is in control, skies are partly sunny to clear, and the cove will see the same quiet, dry weather as the surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight: the Sound (65°F) is already about as warm as the air at 4 PM and ends up nearly 5°F warmer than the air by 7 PM as the evening cools — but there is nothing for it to buffer against.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: strong high pressure (about 1030 mb) sits over the area. The atmosphere has no storm fuel at all — the model shows zero instability through the evening — there are no National Weather Service alerts, and the forecast is simply partly sunny, turning clear. The NWS discussion does not mention showers again until late Tuesday.

About the radar blip: the 3:51 PM radar scan showed one small, strong-looking echo about 38 miles west-southwest, over northern New Jersey. It was not there on the previous scan, and the airports around it (Newark, Caldwell, Teterboro) were all reporting clear or mostly clear skies with no rain at 3:45 PM. With no instability and high pressure overhead, that echo is almost certainly a radar artifact rather than a real shower, so it is not being treated as an approaching storm and no arrival time is given.

Local effects: on summer afternoons the cool Sound often builds a stable layer of air that weakens incoming storms. That is not in play tonight. The water is 65°F and the air is 64–66°F — no gap to speak of — and because the Sound holds its temperature while the air cools after sunset (6:21 PM), the water ends up warmer than the air: roughly 1°F warmer at 5 PM, 4°F at 6 PM and 5°F by 7 PM. The sea breeze is not running either. Neither effect helps or hurts tonight.

Most likely outcome: dry and quiet at the cove and in every neighboring town, with light easterly air and temperatures sliding from the mid 60s into the upper 50s by 10 PM.

What would change the call: the New Jersey echo persisting on later scans and moving east, or rain actually being reported at the airports underneath it. Neither is expected.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander

hourly.shift_note: right shift continuing, puffs fading after sunset

wind.tactics_blurb: Drifter-class light easterly that slowly swings right (ENE to ESE) through the evening, with Greenwich Point blanketing the east side of the course. Favor the right, open-water side for both the shift and the better pressure, keep the boat moving, and stay out of the lee of the point.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of day: a light gradient-wind evening — no sea breeze in play. A sea breeze needs the land to be at least 5°F warmer than the water, and today the air–water temperature difference is essentially zero (air 64–66°F, Sound 65°F). What is blowing is the weak background flow around high pressure: the well-sited airport and buoy sensors average only about 6 kt, from the east to southeast.

What the cove actually has: the Riverside YC station read ESE 3.5 kt at 4 PM, with a 10-minute average of just 2.2 kt and puffs to 6–7. The model has 5–6 kt over open water, and the western-Sound buoy agreed with that at last report (E 5.6 kt, about 75 minutes old). The gap is geography, not a model miss: an easterly comes across Greenwich Point, which shelters the cove more than any other direction. The hourly numbers above are therefore shaded about 1–2 kt below the model.

Shifts through the window: the model swings the breeze slowly and steadily right — ENE (075°) at 5 PM, east at 6 PM, ESE (105–120°) from 7 to 8 PM — then lets it ease back a little to about 105° by 10 PM. That is a persistent shift of roughly 45° rather than an oscillation to tack on. On top of it, expect short-term wandering of 20° or more: nearby stations disagree widely on direction right now, which is typical when the flow is this weak.

Favored side: right. Looking upwind, the right is the open-water side toward the cove mouth, away from the wind shadow of Greenwich Point, and it is also the inside of the persistent right shift. As the breeze goes further toward the southeast after 7 PM the shelter eases slightly, with the best pressure along the western side of the course.

Will it hold: yes, in the sense that it will not get worse — this wind is not driven by the sun, so sunset (6:21 PM) does not switch it off. But there is no build coming either: 3–5 kt all evening, with the puffs flattening out after dark as the air near the water cools. For the fleet that means marginal, patience-testing racing: priority on boat speed and connecting puffs over fine positioning, and long glassy holes near the east shore.

data_caveats: Radar showed a single strong echo 38 mi WSW over northern New Jersey at 3:51 PM; it was absent on the prior scan, airports beneath it report clear skies, and the model shows zero instability — treated as a radar artifact, not an approaching storm, so no arrival time is published
The main forecast-model run only reached 7 PM when data was pulled; the 8 PM hour was filled in from the same run a few minutes later and 9–10 PM come from the previous hour's run
Gust values are estimated from the Riverside YC gust-to-average ratio — the model wind output has no gust field
Hourly speeds are shaded 1–2 kt below the model to reflect Greenwich Point's shelter in an easterly (RYC reading 2–4 kt vs. model 5 kt)
Buoy 44040 (western Sound) reading is 75 min old; Sound water temperature comes from Bridgeport Harbor (BRHC3)
